extracted.intended_audience: researchers, editors, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions (particularly in mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: A blog-category page compiling short news items about retractions, expressions of concern, and publication-integrity problems affecting mathematics and related fields; each item summarizes causes and context for retractions. Useful for tracking reasons papers are withdrawn and patterns of misconduct or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper may be retracted for 'significant overlap' with a previous paper (including one by the same authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction example: paper pulled because it had 'significant overlap' with a previous paper by the same authors; overlap plus failure to reference the earlier work can trigger retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cite or acknowledge related work
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers must cite and acknowledge related prior studies; failing to do so (even for related work by the same authors) is grounds for retraction or criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: retraction notice cited that the authors 'didn’t cite or acknowledge the other study.' Authors' omission of references to their own prior related study prompted the retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism (including from unpublished/handwritten sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of material taken from another researcher’s manuscript (even a handwritten manuscript) or otherwise presenting others' work as one's own constitutes plagiarism and can lead to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction note: paper plagiarized from a handwritten manuscript; such similarities may escape automated detection if not word-for-word, but are still misconduct. Journals may investigate and retract when plagiarism is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-duplication / duplicate publication (including publisher duplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate publication — publishing substantially the same paper more than once — can lead to retraction. This includes cases where publishers mistakenly published the same paper twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: publishers accidentally published the same paper twice and retracted one version; the posts question whether a retraction is fair when the duplication was due to publisher error rather than author misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of Concern for methodological/algorithmic issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may issue an Expression of Concern (EOC) when readers raise substantial concerns about algorithms or methodology in a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: PLOS ONE issued an EOC after readers raised concerns about an algorithm; editorial boards may consult and decide an EOC is appropriate. Corrections (e.g., fixing equations) may also be issued if problems are limited to errors rather than misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient methodological transparency / lack of information to justify algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should provide necessary information to justify presented algorithms and make methods clear; lacking such information can provoke concerns or editorial actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may argue that typos caused confusion, but journals expect enough detail to 'justify the presented algorithms.' If methods are unclear, readers and editors may challenge the work and issue corrections or concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of scientific contribution and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paper is judged to lack scientific contributions or novelty, a journal may retract it on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a retraction notice citing 'Lack of scientific contributions and novelty' as the reason for removal from the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship misrepresentation and forged authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Misstatements about who authored a paper (including forged authorship or faked emails) are serious misconduct that can result in retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a paper was retracted when it was discovered the listed authorship was false (a solo author masquerading as multiple authors); journals retract when authorship cannot be substantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding misstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrepresenting funding sources on a manuscript is a serious issue that can trigger retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a retracted study had falsely claimed funding; when funding statements are shown to be untrue, journals may remove the article from the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid/derivative use of previous data without proper attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining original data with material taken from earlier work without appropriate attribution or acknowledgement (a hybrid of old and new material) can be grounds for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an algorithm paper combined original data with material from an earlier paper and was retracted for that overlap; hybrid work must clearly attribute sources and explain novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and sufficiency of retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices should provide sufficient detail about reasons for retraction; sparse or unhelpful notices impede understanding of what went wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes 'retraction notice is sparse on the details' as problematic; better practice is a clear explanation so readers and authors understand the basis for the action.
